blogs.title: When Legends Mislead: Federal Circuit Reverses on Conflicting Signal Mapping in Finesse v. AT&T
blogs.description: The panel’s reversal on the ’134 patent turns on an expert’s inconsistent mapping of “signals of interest” and “interference generating signals” to a vendor schematic. The court held that Dr. Wells’s testimony—tying the interference signal to a modeled PIM path generated after the RF ADC—could not support a finding that the receiver sampled both signals, and his later pivot to generic x1/x2 inputs lacked a clear mapping to the claim terms. Drawing on Johns Hopkins v. Datascope, the opinion underscores that self-contradictory expert testimony cannot sustain a verdict. This post analyzes the evidentiary failure, how reliance on annotated OEM documents can backfire, and practical trial lessons for proving element-by-element sampling in signal-processing cases.

blogs.title: Counting to Seven: Numeric Claim Limits and the Perils of Partial Proof in Signal-Processing Patents
blogs.description: The ’775 patent required seven specified third-order multiplications of three signals. Finesse showed only three distinct multiplications in Nokia documentation, and those involved modulus and complex conjugates rather than the claimed products. The Federal Circuit found no substantial evidence of all seven multiplications or a coherent mapping. This post unpacks the court’s insistence on exact compliance with numeric limitations, the hazards of inferring repetition or equivalence from high-level math blocks, and best practices for proving algorithmic steps in DSP claims (think source code, test vectors, and explicit operation logs).

blogs.title: No Clear Disavowal: “Three Signals” as Separately Identifiable, Not Unique—Drafting and Litigation Lessons
blogs.description: Although the court reversed on infringement, it rejected the argument that prosecution amendments limited the ’775 patent to three unique input signals. Relying on Continental Circuits, the panel found no clear and unambiguous disavowal; the most the record showed was a requirement for three separately identifiable signals. This post explores the construction’s doctrinal significance, the limited weight of inventor testimony, how to draft around “unique” versus “identifiable” inputs in DSP claims, and what litigators should do to preserve (and prove) uniqueness limits if they matter to noninfringement.

blogs.title: Substantial Evidence with Teeth: The Federal Circuit’s Renewed Policing of Expert Testimony
blogs.description: Applying Fifth Circuit JMOL standards but Federal Circuit substantial-evidence review for infringement, the panel reversed two verdicts for lack of coherent expert proof. Citing Apple v. Wi-LAN and Johns Hopkins v. Datascope, the opinion fits a pattern: juries cannot rely on ambiguous mappings or contradictions to bridge claim gaps. This post situates Finesse within a broader trend of heightened scrutiny of complex technical testimony, explains how such reversals emerge from sparse or inconsistent records, and offers appellate-preservation tips for both sides in E.D. Tex. trials.

blogs.title: Damages on a House of Cards: $166 Million Lump Sum Vacated After JMOL Reversal
blogs.description: Because noninfringement compelled reversal on both asserted patents, the court vacated the life-of-patent lump-sum damages award and taxed costs against the plaintiff. This post examines why the panel did not remand on damages, the fragility of portfolio-wide or feature-based lump sums when infringement fails on individual elements, and how to structure damages models and apportionment evidence to survive if liability falters on some asserted claims.

blogs.title: The Road Not Taken: Unreached Constructions of “Receiver” and “Co-Located” in Interference-Cancellation Claims
blogs.description: The panel declined to reach disputed constructions of “receiver” in the ’134 patent and “co-located” in the ’775 patent after reversing on sufficiency grounds. This post explores the latent stakes of those terms in radio architectures, how future litigants might frame them given this record, and why preserving alternative claim-construction theories remains critical even when a case seems to rise or fall on technical proofs.

blogs.title: Customer-Suit Dynamics in the 5G Era: OEM Intervention, Evidence Control, and Strategic Risk
blogs.description: AT&T faced claims based on Nokia radios, and Nokia intervened. The case spotlights the double-edged nature of OEM technical documents: indispensable for explaining complex features like PIM-C, yet potentially fatal when they do not squarely map to claim elements. This post discusses indemnity and control issues, coordinating expert narratives across carrier and OEM defendants, and how to curate documentation to avoid overreading legends and block diagrams at trial.

blogs.title: From PIM to JMOL: Proving Interference Cancellation in Complex Radios
blogs.description: PIM cancellation is technically intricate, but patent plaintiffs still must present clean, claim-by-claim mappings. This post offers a practitioner’s checklist derived from Finesse: prove where in the signal chain “interference generating signals” actually exist relative to sampling; demonstrate closed-loop phase and amplitude adjustment with sub-sample shifts; and for algorithmic claims, walk the jury through each specified multiplication with concrete artifacts. The takeaway is simple: in DSP-heavy cases, precision beats persuasion.
